questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: From the start, I knew that I wanted to attend a university in the US, as I wanted to ensure the best selection of courses taught in English. Boston is known as one of the best cities to study in due to the sheer number of universities (Harvard, MIT, North-East, Boston College, and Boston University, to name some), creating an internationally vibrant city. Furthermore, Boston University had a great selection of courses, great professors, and an excellent placement.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: BU had done a very good job at providing exchange students with all the information necessary.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: On the first day of the intro-days, they hosted a meeting for students from abroad, providing me with any information  i needed and gave me the possibility to ask any question i wanted to.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was challenging to find housing off-campus. The rent in Boston is costly. I used the side "Blueground" and rented a fully furnished apartment from them. I wanted to rent through a company (and not FB, etc.) since I feared getting scammed - which happens quite often. I lived in North End - it is approximately 30 min from campus, but it was definitely worth it. 
North End is the Italian part of Boston; therefore, there are many good restaurants, bars, etc., in that area. I loved living in North End. The TD-Garden is also in North-End.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off-campus allows you to choose the area, make food yourself, etc. - thus giving you more flexibility. If you are a graduate student and intend to take graduate-level courses, be aware that most people from graduate classes live off campus. However, if you want to take courses on an undergraduate level, most student lives on-campus - therefore, you might miss some of the social connections and social events if you live off-campus. That said, the on-campus housing is not always as good as you could hope for, and exchange students seem to be placed last.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You are given access to a portal where you can register for classes and are allowed to take (almost) any classes you want - if you live up to the requirements and there is space left in the class.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The exchange coordinator is very helpfull and will try to get you into the classes you want to attend

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to register for 5/6 classes I wanted to attend.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Even if you are not qualified for a class you want to take, talk to the professor and ask if they will allow you into a class anyways. Sometimes you have another course from your UCPH that will qualify you even though you didn't take the qualifying course at BU. The exchange coordinator will also gladly help with this.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some of the classes had a very demanding workload. I took an extra class for enjoyment, and I would not necessarily recommend this - at least if you only attend graduate-level courses as I did. As far as I heard, there is a big difference in the workload of graduate and undergraduate courses, so if you want to attend more classes than required, mixing in some undergraduate classes might be a good idea.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The processors at BU strive to create a relationship with the students and have open office hours that the student widely uses - in addition, many of the classes (in particular graduate classes) was smaller than the ones at UCPH. Furthermore, the courses had a lot of assignments throughout the semester, making up the final grade. Thus, it was very different than at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Political Risk Analysis
Intelligence Issues 
Political Campaigns 
Digital Diplomacy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend Political Risk Analysis. Professor Oates is very vibrant and seems like he enjoys teaching. Furthermore, his course is oriented toward the real world, not just academia

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There is (almost) no way around paying approximately 1200 for insurance at BU.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I was shocked by how expensive everything is - grocery shopping was almost double the price compared to Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They have unbelievably many clubs. BU has a club for anything you can think of.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you want to do volunteer work, sports, theater, language, journalism, or anything else, attend the Splash event, where all clubs are in attendance. Furthermore, I recommend that students take advantage of the facilities, such as the SportsCenter, which also has a pool. My nr. 1 recommendation would be to get sports-pass and attend games. In particular, hockey games are a lot of fun since BU has one of the grates hockey teams in all of America - some games are even played at TD Garden.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend going to a basket game with the Celtics at TD Garden and a hockey game with the Boston Bruins. It is expensive but worth it.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy - not that different compared to Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Attend sports games and other social gatherings. You can also join a club and meet people interested in the same thing as you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really anything to be honest

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The sports-culture

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
It will be expensive, but worth it. 
Do yourself a favor and apply for grants - many of them are available for US students. 
Do attend the games - it is so much fun.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be aware that the winters in Boston are freezing! Even colder than you think.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The professors are fascinating, and almost all of them have had a career outside academia, making the lecture incredibly interesting.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I took four graduate-level courses, and I think that is was a big work-load. If I had a redo, I would have mixed in an undergraduate class or stuck to the recommended three courses.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
